p2.2: Forward planning for the student (11/21-11/22/26)¶

Part of phase 2: p2_summary.ipynb connects this notebook with p2.1-p2.3.

Note (11/24/26): the network has since lost its dest head (here it gave relevance, the start network's AND-OR ordering, and dest_quality.py's measures; relevance added nothing). This notebook's results were made with it, and its saved outputs stand; to rerun the cells that compute tables here (they use the dest head and the old start), check out tag pre-dest-removal. Since then AND-OR is ordered by the policy head and sessions start from paths.START, an apprentice trained without a dest head (p2_summary.ipynb, section 7).

The fitted student plays by intuition alone: on every board it samples a move from its policy head (MODEL.md). AND-OR's backward reasoning is only its teacher in pretraining. The question here is whether a heuristically guided forward planner - short rollouts, judged by how much new and goal-relevant ground they cover - is a good candidate for what people add as they gain expertise, and where expertise would enter it.

Two ingredients:

  • Novelty (Lipovetzky & Geffner's width-based planning): a feature is one car in one place on its lane; a rollout earns credit for features no board of the attempt has had yet.
  • Relevance: the network's dest head scores every feature on the current board by how soon a solution from here puts that car there (target 0.8^(k-1) at k moves into the route, 0 if never); r(f) = sigmoid(dest). It is "how likely this new position is to be on the way to the goal".

This notebook reads tables written by experiments/dest_quality.py and experiments/forward.py (models/summary); sections 1.3 and 1.4 compute their tables here.

In [1]:

import pandas as pd

from rushhour import paths

SUMMARY = os.path.join(paths.MODELS, "summary")
INK, MUTED, RULE, GRID = "#1f1f1d", "#5f5e5a", "#b5b4ad", "#e6e5e0"
TEACHERS = {"no_teacher": ("no teacher", "#8a8a85"), "bayes4_0.45": ("bayes4", "#2a78d6"),
            "random_0.3": ("random 30%", "#e6a00d"), "random_1.0": ("random 100%", "#e6550d")}
plt.rcParams.update({"font.size": 9, "axes.titlesize": 10, "axes.titlelocation": "left", "figure.dpi": 110,
                     "legend.frameon": False, "legend.fontsize": 8.5})


def tidy(ax, grid="y"):
    for side in ("top", "right"):
        ax.spines[side].set_visible(False)
    for side in ("left", "bottom"):
        ax.spines[side].set_color(RULE)
    ax.tick_params(colors=MUTED)
    if grid:
        ax.grid(axis=grid, color=GRID, lw=0.8)
    ax.set_axisbelow(True)

1. Is the relevance map any good, and does it sharpen with experience?¶

Truth comes from breadth-first search: for every board, the optimal-route DAG, and for every feature the fewest moves k at which some optimal route first puts that car there (none if no optimal route does). Boards: the 100 held-out puzzles of the AND-OR apprentice (1-30 moves), each start plus 2 boards 3 random moves off it and 2 boards 8 random moves off it (500 boards). About 35% of a board's ~40 features lie on some optimal route.

Measures (per board, then averaged; AUC 0.5 = chance):

  • on-route AUC: features on some optimal route vs features on none;
  • next-move AUC: features an optimal next move reaches (k = 1) vs the rest;
  • far AUC: features first reached 3+ moves on vs off-route ones - the long-range part rollouts would need;
  • policy optimal: share of boards where the policy head's top move is optimal (the proposals, for comparison).

Next-move relevance is learned within about three epochs and then stops. Far relevance stays at about 0.68 through round 1 (more epochs of copying plain AND-OR do not help) and rises in rounds 2 and 3, where the expert is AND-OR ordered by the network and its routes are shorter: the long-range map comes from better routes to learn from. Off-route boards (3 or 8 random moves off the start) give nearly the same numbers:

1.2 Within a session¶

The same measures for the session students (run aostart_free_m10_s2_agency1: seed 2, ΔA 1, 8 students per teacher), at every saved snapshot.

With no teacher, far AUC rises 0.67 → 0.72 while next-move AUC and the policy's top move stay flat; teachers that show more moves sharpen it further (random 100%: 0.79). One seed, 8 students per teacher; no standard errors.

1.3 What the values look like¶

AUC only measures ranking. In a score that sums relevance, the scale matters too. Features of the 100 start boards, grouped by when the nearest optimal route first needs them:

In [6]:
sys.path.insert(0, os.path.join("..", "experiments"))
import torch
import dest_quality as dq_mod
from rushhour.student import PolicyAgent
from rushhour.student.labels import _destinations, _move_index

starts = [it for it in dq_mod.boards() if it["kind"] == "start"]
rows = []
for name, path in [("start", paths.START),
                   ("round 3", os.path.join(paths.APPRENTICE, "gamma0.07_free", "round3_epoch03.pt"))]:
    agent = PolicyAgent.load(path)
    for it in starts:
        b = it["board"]
        sd, dest = dict(b), agent._evaluate(b)[1]
        for car, d, s, moved in _destinations(b, (6, 6), agent.max_slide):
            k = it["first"].get((car, moved))
            r = torch.sigmoid(dest[_move_index(sd, car, d, s, 6, agent.max_slide)]).item()
            rows.append({"network": name, "k": k or 0, "r": r})
feat = pd.DataFrame(rows)
feat["needed"] = pd.cut(feat.k, [-1, 0, 1, 2, 5, 99], labels=["never (off route)", "next move (k=1)", "k=2", "k=3-5",
                                                               "k>5"])
calib = feat.groupby(["needed", "network"], observed=True).r.mean().unstack().round(3)
calib.insert(0, "target", [0, 1, 0.8, None, None])
calib.insert(0, "share", (feat[feat.network == "start"].needed.value_counts(normalize=True).reindex(calib.index)
                          .round(2)))
calib

The ordering is right but the scale is compressed: even features needed on the next move score about 0.3, because the head was trained on one route per board while many exist. Experience mostly widens the gap between needed and unneeded features (next move vs off route: about 4× at the start, 8× at round 3). In a sum, 60% of features are off route at 0.04-0.07 each, so a rollout that pushes five cars somewhere new and irrelevant scores about as much as one that does the thing needed next.

1.4 The value head¶

The third head predicts a board's moves to go (in tens; trained on the moves left on the solved routes it learns from). Nothing in the session reads it. On the 100 start boards: how well it ranks true distances, its typical error, and how often the successor it rates closest to the goal is an optimal move (the policy head's top move is optimal on 85-87% of these start boards):

In [7]:
from scipy.stats import spearmanr
from rushhour import board

SESSION = os.path.join(paths.MODELS, "sessions", "aostart_free_m10_s2_agency1")
VALUE_NETS = {"start": paths.START, "round 3": os.path.join(paths.APPRENTICE, "gamma0.07_free", "round3_epoch03.pt"),
              "student, no teacher (s0, 720)": os.path.join(SESSION, "no_teacher", "student00_puzzle720.pt"),
              "student, random 100% (s0, 720)": os.path.join(SESSION, "random_1.0", "student00_puzzle720.pt")}
succ = []
for it in starts:
    b = it["board"]
    dist = board.multi_bfs(b)
    nxt = [s for _, s in board.neighbors(b, board.car_orientations(b))]
    succ.append((nxt, [dist[s] == it["distance"] - 1 for s in nxt]))
rows = {}
for name, path in VALUE_NETS.items():
    agent = PolicyAgent.load(path)
    agent.net.eval()

    def moves_to_go(states):
        with torch.no_grad():
            return 10 * agent.net.heads(torch.stack([agent.encoder.encode(s) for s in states]))[2].numpy()

    pred, true = moves_to_go([it["board"] for it in starts]), np.array([it["distance"] for it in starts])
    rows[name] = {"spearman with distance": spearmanr(pred, true).statistic,
                  "mean abs error (moves)": np.abs(pred - true).mean(),
                  "closest-rated successor optimal": np.mean([opt[int(np.argmin(moves_to_go(nxt)))]
                                                              for nxt, opt in succ])}
pd.DataFrame(rows).T.round(3)

spearman with distance mean abs error (moves) closest-rated successor optimal
start 0.633 12.803 0.78
round 3 0.769 4.392 0.78
student, no teacher (s0, 720) 0.661 4.480 0.85
student, random 100% (s0, 720) 0.667 3.821 0.81

It ranks boards moderately (spearman 0.63-0.77) and, used greedily, picks an optimal move on 78-85% of start boards, about as often as the policy (85-87%). Over all 500 boards, including those off the route, it does worse: 57-68%, against the policy's 75% (a check run outside this notebook). The start's absolute error is large: AND-OR's routes are long, so "moves left" is inflated; the session's own shorter routes pull it down.

2. The forward planner¶

experiments/forward.py, solve_forward. Every turn, on board b:

  1. relevance: the dest head on b gives r(f) for every feature;
  2. proposals: K rollouts of up to D moves, each move sampled from the policy head at temperature 1 (never back to one of the last 10 boards of the attempt or to a board earlier in the rollout, if it can avoid it);
  3. evaluation: a rollout that solves the puzzle wins (the shortest); otherwise its score is the sum of r(f) over the features it reaches that no board of the attempt has had, each counted once;
  4. the first move of the best rollout is played (the first sampled, on a tie).

How strict novelty is. Two mechanisms, only one of which forbids anything:

  • Hard, over whole boards (the session student's own rule): a move back to one of the last 10 boards of the attempt is removed from the options - for the move played and for every rollout step - and, inside a rollout, so is a move back to any of its earlier boards; if every move would, all are allowed again.
  • Soft, over features (the planner's score): no feature is forbidden. A feature seen anywhere in the attempt is worth 0 from then on (no fading); a new one gets its full relevance. It only ranks the K rollouts: if none reaches anything new, they all score 0 and the first sampled one is played - a plain policy sample (the "ties" below). A pruning version, as in Iterated Width, would instead discard such rollouts.

K = 1 is the session student's intuition exactly. Test: 100 of the session's held-out puzzles (25 per bin of 9-11, 14-16, 19-21 and 24-26 moves), 2 runs each, cap max(50, 10 × optimal), no giving up. Score: moves/optimal with an unsolved puzzle counted at its cap (lower is better). Networks: the start, round 3 of pretraining, and the 8 students of the no-teacher and random-100% teachers after 720 puzzles (same session run as 1.2).

Conditions:

  • novelty only: every r(f) = 1;
  • no attempt memory: a feature counts as new if it isn't on b (the current board), so relevance acts as a pure lookahead evaluator;
  • uniform: rollout moves drawn uniformly from the legal ones, so the network acts only through relevance (and "uniform, novelty only" uses no network at all);
  • K16 D8: more and deeper rollouts;
  • value: rollouts ranked by the value head's moves to go at their end board (fewest first), no novelty;
  • novelty then value: novelty count first, the value head breaking ties (best-first width search ranks by novelty, then a goal heuristic).

In [9]:
CONTRASTS = [("does relevance help, given policy proposals?", "K8 D4", "K8 D4 novelty only"),
             ("does relevance help, given uniform proposals?", "K8 D4 uniform", "K8 D4 uniform novelty only"),
             ("do policy proposals help (novelty only)?", "K8 D4 novelty only", "K8 D4 uniform novelty only"),
             ("does search help the policy?", "K8 D4", "intuition"),
             ("does a bigger search help?", "K16 D8", "K8 D4"),
             ("value alone vs intuition (policy proposals)", "K8 D4 value", "intuition"),
             ("value alone vs novelty (policy proposals)", "K8 D4 value", "K8 D4 novelty only"),
             ("does value help novelty, breaking ties? (policy)", "K8 D4 novelty then value", "K8 D4 novelty only"),
             ("does value help novelty, breaking ties? (uniform)", "K8 D4 uniform novelty then value",
              "K8 D4 uniform novelty only")]


def contrast(g, a, b):
    """Mean difference a - b; ± is the SE over the 8 students, or for one network over its 200 attempts."""
    x, y = fw[(fw.group == g) & (fw.condition == a)], fw[(fw.group == g) & (fw.condition == b)]
    if x.network.nunique() > 1:
        d = x.groupby("network").ratio.mean() - y.groupby("network").ratio.mean()
        return f"{d.mean():+.2f} ± {d.std() / np.sqrt(len(d)):.2f}"
    se = np.sqrt(x.ratio.var() / len(x) + y.ratio.var() / len(y))
    return f"{x.ratio.mean() - y.ratio.mean():+.2f} ± {se:.2f}"


pd.DataFrame({GROUPS[g]: {q: contrast(g, a, b) for q, a, b in CONTRASTS} for g in GROUPS})

The students' ± understates the uncertainty: every student played the same 100 puzzles with the same seeds, so the noise of that one sample (about ±0.25 per condition) is shared and not counted. With uniform proposals, relevance may help slightly for the session students (−0.12, −0.19), but not for round 3, whose map is the sharpest, so I read it as no reliable effect.

One score: novelty and value combined, with fading memory¶

"Novelty, then value" ranks strictly: value only matters when novelty ties. A person would more plausibly fold both into one judgment ("I haven't been here before, so I must be getting somewhere"):

score = λ × novelty − moves to go (value head, at the rollout's end)

λ is how many moves of predicted progress one new feature is worth: λ = 0 is value alone, λ → ∞ is the strict order. Novelty can also fade: a feature last on the attempt's boards age moves ago counts 1 − 0.5^(age / half-life) (1 if never seen, 0 on the current board), so a placement seen long ago detracts less than one seen recently; an infinite half-life never forgets (all runs before this one).

python experiments/forward.py sweep → forward_sweep.csv: λ from 0.5 to 32 with policy and uniform proposals, and half-lives of 5, 20 and 80 moves at λ 4 and 16 (policy proposals). The students here are 4 per teacher (s0-s3), so the anchors below are recomputed on those 4.

LAMS = [0.5, 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32]

for ax, prefix, title in [(axes[0], "K8 D4", "policy proposals"), (axes[1], "K8 D4 uniform", "uniform proposals")]:

        d = sw[sw.group == g]

        v = d[d.condition == f"{prefix} value"].ratio.mean()

        ax.plot([48], [strict], color=color, marker="D", ms=5)
    ax.set_xscale("log", base=2)
    ax.set_xticks([0.25] + LAMS + [48], ["value\nonly"] + [str(x) for x in LAMS] + ["strict\norder"])
    ax.set_xlabel("λ: moves of predicted progress one new feature is worth")
    ax.set_title(title)
    tidy(ax)
axes[0].set_ylabel("moves / optimal")
axes[0].legend()
fig.suptitle("One combined score matches the strict order once a new feature is worth about 8 moves", x=0.01,
             ha="left", fontsize=10)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

λ 4 half-life never 3.12 2.64 2.81 2.29
half-life 80 3.10 2.55 2.83 2.27
half-life 20 2.99 2.66 2.80 2.32

λ 16 half-life never 2.73 2.47 2.76 2.21
half-life 80 2.52 2.47 2.64 2.10
half-life 20 2.70 2.52 2.73 2.14
half-life 5 2.88 2.56 2.92 2.42
  • The combined score costs nothing once λ is about 8 or more. At λ 8 it is level with the strict order (students +0.01 ± 0.02 and +0.07 ± 0.05; start and round 3 within ±0.3), and flat up to 32. Below 4 it loses (λ 2: +0.3 to +0.7): value then outweighs novelty and the planner circles as value alone does. So the human-like, compensatory version is viable, provided a new placement counts for a lot.
  • No clear sign that experience moves the best λ. Every network is best somewhere in 8-32. The start loses most at low λ (+0.71 at λ 2, against +0.33 to +0.39), as if it should trust its value head least - but its value head's scale is inflated (1.4), so the same λ weighs novelty less for it; the units are not comparable across networks.
  • Fading memory is free over tens of moves, harmful over a few. A half-life of 80 moves is at least as good as never forgetting (λ 16: students −0.12 ± 0.05 and −0.11 ± 0.07, start −0.22 ± 0.25); 20 is about level; 5 hurts (+0.08 to +0.20). Performance therefore does not pin the half-life down within a wide range - people's revisits must (when, after leaving a placement, they come back to it).

What the planner shows¶

  • Search with attempt-level novelty roughly halves moves/optimal for every network, and more search (K16 D8) helps further. The gain over intuition shrinks as the network gains experience (−2.9 at the start, −1.3 at round 3), mostly because intuition itself gets better.
  • All of the network's contribution comes through proposals. Policy instead of uniform proposals is worth 2.5-3.3; relevance is worth nothing measurable, whether the policy proposes (where it could be redundant) or uniform proposals leave it the network's only input. Without attempt memory, relevance as a lookahead evaluator is no better than intuition.
  • Blind novelty search is about as good as a novice's instinct (5.64 vs the start's 5.98); the two together halve the moves.
  • A board evaluator helps where relevance could not: on novelty's ties. The value head alone is a weak guide (better than intuition, 0.8-1.4 worse than novelty: greedy on a noisy value circles). Breaking novelty's ties with it - the turns where no rollout reaches anything new - helps a little with policy proposals (−0.1 to −0.4) and a lot with uniform ones (5.64 → 4.2-4.5). Summed relevance cannot act on those turns: every rollout scores 0. Its gain is about the same for every network, so the value head is not where experience shows up either.
  • Strict or compensatory makes no difference to performance once a new feature is worth 8+ moves of value, and novelty can fade over tens of moves at no cost: both choices are for people's data to make.
  • Novelty search is strong enough that adding it to the start student would break the fitted start: a novice's search budget would have to be near zero and grow with practice.

2b. Forward and backward together¶

People's revisits (notebooks/p2.3_human_likeness.ipynb) ask for no novelty and a soft board memory (β 2, half-life 1), so from here the planner ranks candidates by the value head alone. Backward reasoning joins as a second source of candidates: each turn, backward=N adds N AND-OR passes from the current board (ordered by the dest head with Gumbel noise, lapse rate γ) to the k policy rollouts - a whole plan to the goal, or the moves made until a lapse. All candidates are judged alike (a solving one wins; otherwise the end board's predicted moves to go) and the first move of the best is played.

python experiments/forward.py integrate → forward_integrate.csv (held-out pool puzzles, as above; 4 students per teacher):

  • The two sources complement each other. At the same 8 candidates per turn, 4 rollouts + 4 AND-OR passes beat 8 rollouts (by 0.25-0.56 moves / optimal) and 4 passes (by 0.4-0.8) for every network, and backward plans win about half the turns. More passes help backward reasoning alone (4 vs 1: −0.65 to −1.3).
  • Without novelty the planner is much weaker on these puzzles than the novelty planner above (start: 4.88 against about 2.7): the price of matching people's revisits.
  • On the human layouts (p2.3_human_likeness.ipynb's table and the shared-γ fit below) the mix is efficient (1.85 × optimal, people 2.09) but restless: it returns to an earlier board on 13.6% of moves and undoes 9% (people 9.7%, 5.6%), because the soft memory shapes only the policy rollouts - each turn's fresh AND-OR pass can resolve a subgoal differently and move a car straight back.

One lapse rate for both¶

AND-OR's γ is the chance of losing a subgoal chain at each step. The rollouts get the same kind of limit: each simulated move past the first continues with probability 1 − γ (rollout_gamma; capped at 20 moves). python experiments/fit_memory.py gamma → gamma_fit.csv: the mixed planner (4 + 4, value, soft memory) on the 70 human layouts, 10 runs each, over the rollouts' γ × AND-OR's γ (0.03-0.3); the diagonal is one shared γ. Misfit to people: skill (chance of an optimal move by distance to the goal, and moves / optimal when solved) plus revisits (board and car returns by age, matched attempts).

  • γ cannot fix the shape of people's skill. Every setting is too good near the goal (99% optimal moves 2-3 moves out, people 87%; 86% even in their first 10 trials) and too poor mid-puzzle (31-43% at 7-9 moves out, people 54%, 48% in their first 10 trials). γ trades these off only a little. Near the goal people make many moves that leave the distance unchanged (10% of their moves there); mid-puzzle they choose better than the start network's value head lets the planner. A lapse at the level of the move played, and a better value head, are the candidates.
  • The share of turns won by backward plans stays at 44-49% whatever the γs.

Backward plans and the memory¶

Where the mixed planner's undos come from, and three fixes (solve_forward's candidate_memory and commit):

  • candidate memory × c: the soft memory also judges the candidates. A candidate whose first move leads back to a board the attempt had age moves ago is ranked as if c × β × 0.5^(age / half-life) moves further from the goal (with β 2, half-life 1, an undo costs c / 2 moves: × 4 is 2 moves).
  • commit to plan: once a backward plan is played, the student keeps to it without deliberating, each later move with probability 1 − γ (the shared lapse), until it ends or lapses.
  • plan stays a candidate: the rest of the plan joins the next turn's candidates, judged alike.

python experiments/fit_memory.py undo → undo_fit.csv: the mixed planner (4 + 4, value, soft memory, shared γ 0.03) on the 70 human layouts, 10 runs each. Misfits as in the γ fit; undo and returns on matched attempts (1.5-3 × optimal, solved); the source rows are over all moves.

  • The undos come from backward plans. In the plain mixed planner a quarter of the moves taken from a fresh AND-OR pass undo the move before (25.6%), against 9.9% of moves from rollouts. Each turn's pass starts over from the board, and the network ordering, with Gumbel noise, often resolves the last subgoal the other way.
  • Letting the memory judge the candidates fixes it. At × 4 (an undo counts as 2 moves further from the goal) the planner undoes 5.4% of matched moves and returns to a board 9.6% of the time - people 5.6% and 9.7% - and the revisit misfit falls from 0.060 to 0.014 with the skill misfit unchanged (best overall, 0.093). × 16 overshoots (2.4% undos). Backward moves still undo 11% of the time, rollouts 4.5%.
  • Commitment does not. Following a plan to its end or a lapse leaves undos at 7.9%: plans themselves move a car back (9% of committed moves undo - clearing the way for one car, then another), and when the plan lapses the next fresh pass can still undo. It does make the student more efficient (1.75 × optimal, people 2.09) and better mid-puzzle (49% optimal at 7-9 moves, people 54%), so the skill misfit worsens on balance. With the candidate memory added (commit + × 4) it fits revisits best (0.012) but skill a little worse (0.090 against 0.080).
  • None of these touch the skill shape: still 98-100% optimal 2-3 moves from the goal (people 87%).

Learning over the session: γ by stage¶

van Opheusden et al. fitted their model to successive blocks of play and found expertise as deeper search and fewer lapses. The same question here, with the one shared lapse rate γ standing for how far ahead the student holds a thought: python experiments/fit_memory.py learning → gamma_learning.csv runs the mixed planner (4 + 4, value, soft memory, no candidate memory - this ran alongside the undo fix) over γ 0.01-0.3 (rollouts capped at 40 moves) on the 70 human layouts, 10 runs each. Each stage of people's session (trials 1-10, 11-20, 21-35, 36+) is fitted separately, the model's attempts weighted by how often people at that stage played each layout; the misfit is the γ fit's (skill + revisits) against that stage's people.

  • The fit moves toward small γ - longer-held thoughts - with practice, as van Opheusden's players searched deeper. The best γ is 0.03 in trials 1-10 and 11-20 and 0.01 from trial 21 on; more robust than the minimum (the curves are noisy, 10 runs per layout) is the slope: in trials 1-10 every γ fits about equally (misfit 0.11-0.15), while by trials 36+ a high γ costs a lot (0.3: 0.30 against 0.11). Early people look like a planner whose depth isn't pinned down; later people rule out the shallow one.
  • Efficiency is what γ captures. People's moves / optimal falls 2.31 → 1.96 over the session, and the model spans about that range from γ 0.3 to 0.01 (2.33 → 1.98 on trials 1-10's layouts).
  • Mid-puzzle skill is what it can't. People's optimal-move chance 7-9 moves out rises 48% → 59%; the model tops out near 45-47% at the smallest γ. Deeper thought with the same start network's judgement can't reach later people, so part of their learning must be in the judgement itself (the network's policy and value heads) - the session student's training does that, and fitting a per-stage network alongside γ is the next step.
  • Caveats: people who reach trial 36+ are partly the more persistent players; one start network; the runs use the planner without the candidate memory (revisits are a little too frequent throughout).

Judgement or depth: the session student's own networks¶

γ alone can't reach later people's mid-puzzle skill with the start network's judgement. The session student does learn judgement: the calibrated session (ao_people_all_m10: 8 students, ×10, full hindsight, fitted to people's learning rate; the snapshots are in the archive) saved each student's network after 18, 36 and 54 of people's trials. python experiments/fit_memory.py snapshots → gamma_snapshots.csv: each snapshot plays the 70 layouts by intuition (as in the session: the hard 10-board memory) and in the mixed planner (as in the γ-by-stage fit) at γ 0.01, 0.03, 0.1, 0.3, one run per student and layout. Each stage of people's session is paired with the snapshot at its middle: trials 1-9 with the start network, 10-27 with 18 trials' snapshot, 28-45 with 36, 46+ with 54.

  • The session's learning barely carries into the planner's mid-puzzle skill. With each stage's own snapshot, the planner's chance of an optimal move 7-9 moves out (at its best γ) rises from 45% to 49% by trial 46+, while the start network stays at 45% and people go 48% → 59%. Even the best any snapshot does at any γ is about 52% (γ 0.01). The snapshots improve intuition (moves / optimal 3.85 → 3.09 on these layouts), but mostly by wandering less, not by choosing better mid-puzzle (31% → 34%).
  • The snapshots fit people worse than the start network does, mostly through revisits: in the planner they undo more (8-10% of matched moves against the start network's 7%; people 5-6%), and the gap grows with the snapshot (stage 46+: misfit 0.21 against 0.10). On skill alone they are no better (0.08-0.11, against the start network's 0.07-0.11). Why they undo more is not checked here; a candidate is that the dest head, which orders the AND-OR passes, is trained in the session on an intuitive student's wandering routes.
  • With the snapshots, the best γ barely moves (0.03 through trial 45, 0.01 after), where with the start network it falls to 0.01 from trial 10. So γ falling over the session is not an artefact of a frozen network - but this test doesn't settle what replaces it, because the session's learning makes the planner neither better nor more human.
  • What it says about the design: judgement learned while playing by intuition is the wrong judgement for a planner. If people's mid-puzzle gains are judgement, it has to be learned from the planner's own experience (training the session student with the planner in the loop), or the heads the planner reads (value, dest) need targets that don't come from an intuitive student's wandering.
  • Caveats: one calibrated session (8 students); intuition here runs without giving up, so its moves / optimal is higher than the calibration's; the planner runs use no candidate memory (as in the γ-by-stage fit).

2c. Planning in the session, and how people combine modes¶

Section 2b's planner (4 rollouts + 4 AND-OR passes, best of 8 judged by the value head) is fitted to people's revisits, but it is a constant, heavy deliberation and it has never learned from its own play. This section (11/22/26):

  1. puts the planner in the session loop, so the network learns from the planner's own experience;
  2. asks which planner can start where people do (their first 10 trials), across ways of combining forward and backward reasoning: best of 8, forward rollouts alone, a flat one-move look (Collins et al.'s novices), flat with one checking rollout, and an impasse switch (flat forward, AND-OR plans at an impasse);
  3. looks at people's move times, and fits a move-by-move mixture of intuition and flat planning to people's moves per stage of the session.

Planner in the loop¶

python experiments/planner_session.py reruns the calibrated session (ao_people_all_m10: the same puzzles at people's lengths, order per student, ×10, full hindsight, learning rate, giving up, seed, 8 students) with every puzzle played by the planner (forward.PlannerSolver: 4 rollouts + 4 AND-OR passes, value head, soft memory, candidate memory × 4, γ fixed at 0.03 so that only the network changes). learning_session takes the planner as its solver; labels come from the boards actually played (imagined boards teach nothing). Run planner_people_all_m10; its snapshots are fitted per stage as in the previous section (fit_memory.py snapshots --run planner_people_all_m10 → gamma_snapshots_planner_people_all_m10.csv).

In [19]:
import json


def session_curve(path):
    d = json.load(open(path))
    rows = []
    for lo, hi in [(1, 9), (10, 27), (28, 45), (46, 72)]:
        es = [e for r in d.values() for e in r if lo <= e["trial"] <= hi]
        won = [e for e in es if e["solved"]]
        rows.append({"trials": f"{lo}-{hi}", "solved": np.mean([e["solved"] for e in es]),
                     "moves / optimal (solved)": np.mean([e["moves"] / e["distance"] for e in won])})
    return pd.DataFrame(rows).set_index("trials")

Starting where people do¶

The start network was chosen to match people's first 10 trials (rushhour/surrender.py: the session's 80 held-out puzzles at people's lengths, 10 runs each, no giving up; giving up at the session's scale 0.3 applied afterwards; people: 87.4% ± 2.7% solved, 2.76 ± 0.17 moves / optimal; misfit = squared standard errors). The same calibration for every planner (python experiments/planner_session.py --fit-start / --fit-forward / --fit-flat / --fit-two-mode):

  • best of 8 (4 rollouts + 4 AND-OR passes), γ 0.03-1;
  • forward rollouts alone: k = 2, 3, 4, 8 policy rollouts × γ, judged by the value head;
  • flat (forward.solve_flat): the policy's top m moves looked at one move deep, a softmax over the value head's moves to go / τ - Collins et al.'s flat novice, with consideration limited as in Zhang et al.;
  • flat + check: one checking rollout (≈ 3 moves) from the chosen move; rejected if it ends nowhere better than the current board (up to 2 rejections);
  • impasse switch (forward.solve_two_mode): flat forward by default; at an impasse (a loop back to a board within 10 moves, a 4-move stall in the value head's estimate, or either) one AND-OR pass, followed without deliberating (each step with probability 1 - γ), then back to forward.
In [21]:
from rushhour import human_data as hd, surrender as sr

(hs, hs_se), (hr, hr_se), first10 = sr.human_target(10)
edges, rates, _ = hd.surrender_hazard()
test_puzzles = sr.puzzle_set("test")


def calibrate(df, scale=0.3):
    rows = []
    for c, d in df.groupby("config", sort=False):
        att = {n: [None if m != m else int(m) for m in x.moves] for n, x in d.groupby("puzzle")}
        ps, pr = sr.predict(att, test_puzzles, first10, edges, rates, scale, True)
        row = {"config": c, "solved": ps, "moves / optimal": pr,
               "misfit": ((ps - hs) / hs_se) ** 2 + ((pr - hr) / hr_se) ** 2}
        if "impasses" in d and d.impasses.notna().any():
            row["moves from plans"] = d.backward.sum() / d.played.sum()
            row["impasses / 10 moves"] = 10 * d.impasses.sum() / d.played.sum()
        rows.append(row)
    return pd.DataFrame(rows)


def family(c):
    for prefix, name in [("intuition, hard", "intuition (the calibrated start)"), ("intuition, soft", "intuition, soft memory"),
                         ("best of 8", "best of 8 (4 + 4)"), ("forward", "forward rollouts"),
                         ("flat+check", "flat + check"), ("flat", "flat"), ("two-mode", "impasse switch")]:
        if c.startswith(prefix):
            return name


mixed = pd.read_csv(os.path.join(SUMMARY, "planner_start_fit.csv"))
mixed["config"] = "best of 8, γ " + mixed.gamma.astype(str)
cal = pd.concat([calibrate(mixed)] + [calibrate(pd.read_csv(os.path.join(SUMMARY, f)))
                                      for f in ("forward_start_fit.csv", "flat_start_fit.csv",
                                                "two_mode_start_fit.csv")], ignore_index=True)
cal["family"] = cal.config.map(family)

  • Only intuition starts where people do (misfit 0.1). Everything that deliberates on every move starts too efficient: best of 8 stalls near 1.9 moves / optimal at any γ (the best, γ 0.5, misfits 26.8), because choosing among 8 candidates is itself what makes the student efficient; γ only trades solving for speed.
  • Forward rollouts are viable only when weak: 2 rollouts (misfit 2.4-4.3 at any γ); 3 or more are too good. The number of candidates, not γ, sets the strength.
  • Flat is viable only when it is nearly intuition: the top 3 at τ 4 (misfit 2.2), where the value head hardly counts (a move must look 4 moves closer to be one unit more preferred). A sharp flat choice solves only 46-61% (next cell); considering every move is worse than the policy's top few (the value head is drawn to moves the policy screens out).
  • One checking rollout removes the traps (79-88% solved at any τ) but leaves the student too efficient unless 5 moves are considered at τ 4 (misfit 2.7).
  • The impasse switch rescues the sharp flat choice (70-92% solved; 13-38% of moves from plans, 1-3 impasses per 10 moves) but start too efficient: the best (top 5, τ 1, stall, γ 0.07) solves 87.5% at 2.30 (misfit 7.5), at the weak edge of the grid. AND-OR plans are good, so a student that plans when stuck plays efficiently.

Why a sharp flat choice gets stuck¶

Every 4th of the calibration puzzles (20), one attempt each: the share of moves going back to a board already seen, in the attempts that fail and those that succeed.

In [22]:
import random as _random
import forward
from rushhour.student import PolicyAgent

start_agent = PolicyAgent.load(paths.START)
loops = []
for label, kw in [("flat, top 3, τ 0.25", dict(consider=3, tau=0.25)), ("flat, top 3, τ 4", dict(consider=3, tau=4)),
                  ("flat + check, top 3, τ 0.25", dict(consider=3, tau=0.25, check=True))]:
    for i, (d, s) in enumerate(list(test_puzzles.values())[::4]):
        tr = []
        o = forward.solve_flat(start_agent, s, max(50, 10 * d), rng=_random.Random(i), trace=tr, **kw)
        b = [s] + [x for _, x in tr]
        seen, rev = set(), 0
        for x in b[1:]:
            rev += x in seen
            seen.add(x)
        loops.append({"setting": label, "solved": o["solved"], "revisit share": rev / len(tr),
                      "distinct boards": len(set(b))})
loops = pd.DataFrame(loops)
loops.groupby(["setting", "solved"], sort=False).agg(attempts=("solved", "size"),
                                                     revisit_share=("revisit share", "mean"),
                                                     distinct_boards=("distinct boards", "mean")).round(2)

Failed sharp attempts are loops: 93% of their moves go back to a board already seen, cycling among about 10 boards until the move cap. One move deep, the value head has traps - boards that look better than their neighbours without being on the way out - and the soft memory (an undo costs 0.5) can't break them. Noise (high τ) is one way out; a checking rollout or a backward plan is another.

People's move times¶

From the human profile (moves 2+ from the goal; seconds is the time since the previous move). Speed is relative to each person: quintiles of their own log time, and "slow" = over 2.5 × their median.

Do people shift toward flat planning? A move-by-move mixture¶

python experiments/mode_mixture.py → models/summary/mode_mixture/. Every human move 2+ from the goal gets two exact probabilities from the same network: intuition (the policy's softmax, with the soft memory) and flat planning (the policy's top m moves, a softmax over -moves to go / τ, the memory). A move is (1 - ε) × (w × flat + (1 - w) × intuition) + ε / legal moves; m, τ and ε are fitted over all moves (best: top 5, τ 1), w per stage, per fast / slow move, and per person early (trials 1-27) and late (28+). Intervals: 90%, resampling people. The network is either the start network for every stage, or each stage's own network from the calibrated intuition session (the snapshots above, 8 students' probabilities averaged) - so that a rising w isn't just people's intuition improving. AND-OR plans are not in the mixture: their move probabilities have no closed form, and following a plan depends on a hidden state (whether the person is mid-plan).

  • The rise is in fast moves too (10% → 18%), consistent with the timing data: a fast "propose a few, pick the one that looks closest" mode, used more as the evaluator becomes trustworthy - the reliability-based arbitration of Daw et al. (2005) and Lee et al. (2014): novices don't consult an evaluator that isn't yet worth consulting.
  • Caveats: trials 46+ are the more persistent people (the per-person comparison only partly controls for it); the stage networks are a simulated session's, not each person's; AND-OR is not in the mixture.

Adding backward reasoning: a three-way mixture¶

python experiments/mode_mixture.py andor adds the impasse-switch student's backward mode as a third component: one AND-OR pass from the board (the network's dest head ordering its options with Gumbel noise, lapse rate 0.07), scored by its first move. That probability has no closed form, so it is estimated by sampling passes from every board people played on: 100 with the start network, 25 from each of a stage's 8 snapshots (200 pooled). Each move is scored as the first move of a fresh pass - following a plan made earlier is not modelled. Weights (intuition, flat, AND-OR) on a 0.02 grid, per stage, per distance to the goal and per fast / slow move, with 90% intervals resampling people; flat keeps the two-way fit's top 5 at τ 1, the lapse ε is refitted. No boundary between modes is imposed: distance is a breakdown.

In [25]:

  • People's moves are still mostly intuition-like - 76-88% in every breakdown - and both modes together add little likelihood (at most about 0.04 per move, mid-puzzle).
  • AND-OR does not grow with practice: about 8-10% across stages with the start network; with each stage's network it falls to about 0 in the middle stages, and per person it slightly falls (0.11 → 0.09; 0.06 → 0.04). The practice effect is flat planning's, which again rises from 8% to 18% with the learned networks (per person 0.12 → 0.19).
  • AND-OR is strongest near the goal: 34% (start network) and 26% (stage's) of moves 2-3 from the goal, intervals about 22-38%; flat planning peaks at 4-6 moves out (22%, 28%); far from the goal nearly everything is intuition. But near the goal the three modes predict similar moves - adding flat alone gains as much likelihood there as adding AND-OR alone, or more - so this is suggestive, not decisive.
  • Slow moves are more AND-OR-like (18% and 14%, against 8% and 2% of fast moves), while flat planning lives in fast moves - what the impasse switch predicts if slow moves are impasses.
  • Together: intuition as the base; a fast, flat mid-puzzle mode that grows as the evaluator improves; a slower backward mode for impasses and the end-game that doesn't grow. Caveats: plan following is not modelled (it may claim some of what is credited to intuition); AND-OR's probabilities are sampled (100-200 passes per board); the two network versions settle on different lapse rates (0.01 and 0.1).

When do people reason backward? Loops and slow moves¶

Two tests of when the backward-like moves happen, with the three-way weights refitted per group (90% intervals resampling people; both network versions):

  • After a loop (mode_mixture.py loops → loops.csv): the impasse-switch student turns to AND-OR when a move leads back to a board the attempt had within the last 10 moves. People's loops are observable (the profile's board age); their moves are split into the move on the board a loop just led to, 2-3 moves after, and elsewhere, and by the loop's kind (an undo or a longer return).
  • Plan, then execute (mode_mixture.py slow → slow.csv): if a slow move (over 2.5 × the person's median) is a deliberation that makes a backward plan, the quick moves after it carry it out. Moves are split into the slow move itself, fast moves 1 or 2-3 after the attempt's last slow move (and whether that slow move opened the attempt), and other fast moves.

Each move is scored as the first move of a fresh AND-OR pass, so steps of a plan made earlier that a fresh pass wouldn't pick count against AND-OR: these tests show better what isn't there than prove an absence.

  • Loops don't trigger backward reasoning. The move on the board a loop just led to is less AND-OR-like than moves elsewhere (4% against 10% with the start network; 0% against 4% with the stage's), and more intuition-like (88-90% against 82%) - at every distance, after undos and longer returns alike. People who go in a circle retry the familiar move. Slow moves are AND-OR-like with or without a loop before them (10-20%).
  • No plan is carried out after a slow move. Fast moves 1 or 2-3 after a slow move are no more AND-OR-like than other fast moves (6-8% against 8%; 0-2% against 2%), at every distance. Backward reasoning lives in the slow move itself (18% and 14%; 12-24% across distances with the start network), and the deliberation ends with it.
  • The exception is the opening: when the first move of an attempt is slow, the move after it is backward-like too (14% [10-18] and 8% [4-12], against 4% and 0% after a slow move mid-attempt). The first look at a puzzle seems to produce about two moves of backward reasoning before intuition takes over.
  • Near the goal the backward-like moves are fast (32-40% of fast moves 2-3 from the goal): a short blocking chain is quick to see.
  • So people's backward reasoning looks like one deliberated move at a time - the paper's AND-OR model (one move per search), not this repo's variant (a plan played to its end) or the impasse-switch student's commitment to a plan - and what sets off a slow move is not a loop.

The two-mode student: the mixture as a player¶

forward.solve_lean turns the move-by-move mixture into a student that plays. Each move, independently, it draws one of three modes: with probability w_ao a deliberation (one AND-OR pass from the board, its first move played, no plan kept - the paper's one move per search); with probability w_flat flat planning (the policy's top 5 moves, a softmax over the value head's moves to go, τ 1); otherwise intuition (a policy sample). The soft board memory lowers moves back to recent boards in intuition and flat. opening: the first move of an attempt is always a deliberation and the next is the same pass's second move (people's slow first look and its follow-through). It keeps only what people's moves asked for: no rollouts, no plan following, AND-OR only as single deliberated moves.

Named for its modes: the two-mode student reasons forward (intuition and flat planning) and, now and then, backward (single AND-OR deliberations); the forward student is the same without AND-OR. (In the code they are one solver, forward.solve_lean / forward.LeanSolver, --lean, with w_ao 0 for the forward student; saved runs and tables keep the name lean_*.)

Two comparisons, both with the start network: the start calibration (planner_session.py --fit-lean, as above; flat 0 / 0.08 / 0.18 × AND-OR 0 / 0.1 / 0.2 × opening) and the human profile (fit_memory.py lean → lean_profile.csv: seven variants on the 70 human layouts, 10 runs each, against all of people's play; per mode, its share of moves, how often they are optimal and how often they undo).

To see it choose, move by move, open visualization/p2_two_mode/two_mode_moves.html (built by python experiments/two_mode_animation.py; also embedded in p2_summary, section 6).

  • The two-mode student starts where people do - the first student with planning in it that does: with 8-18% flat and 10-20% AND-OR the misfit is 0.0-1.2 (flat 0.08 + AND-OR 0.2: 0.1; flat 0.18 + AND-OR 0.2: 0.0), close to the mixture's weights; and the value head chooses sharply (τ 1) on the moves flat planning makes. Intuition alone with the soft memory misfits 10.5 (the calibrated start's hard memory: 0.1).
  • AND-OR is not needed for the start: 18% flat alone fits nearly as well (0.6). For the overall level the two modes are partly interchangeable.
  • On the human profile AND-OR does something flat doesn't: at the same 18% of non-intuitive moves, 10% AND-OR + 8% flat beats 18% flat (skill misfit 1.32 against 1.43), mostly near the goal (70% against 65% optimal 2-3 moves out) and in efficiency (3.60 against 3.65); added to the 18%-flat student it helps again (1.43 → 1.18). This is where the mixture puts AND-OR's weight.
  • Per mode: flat moves are the most often optimal (about 46%), AND-OR's next (about 42%), intuition's least (34%); AND-OR moves undo the most (about 15% against 10-11%) - the undo signature of people's slow moves, though people's slow moves are less often optimal than their fast ones, an ordering the model doesn't reproduce.
  • Every variant is far weaker than people's whole session on these layouts (3.5-3.9 moves / optimal against 2.09; 64-72% optimal near the goal against 87%): this is the start network, which finds the human layouts harder than the puzzles it was calibrated on, against people's play from every trial. The differences between variants are the point; the session (with the flat share rising as the mixture found) is the next test.

In the session: the two-mode student (with AND-OR) and the forward student (without)¶

python experiments/planner_session.py --lean plays the calibrated session (ao_people_all_m10's settings) with forward.LeanSolver, its flat share rising over the first 30 trials as people's did in the mixture fit; the network learns from the boards it played, as before. Two runs, each set to start where people do:

  • two-mode, with AND-OR (lean_people_all_m10_ao): flat 8% → 18%, AND-OR 10%, the opening rule (start misfit 0.4);
  • forward, without AND-OR (lean_people_all_m10_noao): flat 18% → 28% (18% is what it needs to start where people do), no AND-OR (start misfit 0.6).

Each run's snapshots (after 18, 36, 54 trials) then play the 70 human layouts with that stage's mode weights, against the same stage of people (fit_memory.py lean-snapshots --run ... → lean_snapshots_<run>.csv).

  • The two-mode student follows people's efficiency gain through the session (2.87 → 2.27 moves / optimal, people 2.77 → 2.17), about as well as the intuition session that was fitted to that curve. The forward student stalls mid-session (2.57 → 2.55) and ends further away (2.36). Both solve slightly less than people (82-84% against 84-89%), probably because the soft memory lets them wander more than the hard 10-board rule.
  • On the human layouts, with AND-OR the fit to each stage of people improves steadily (skill misfit 0.76 → 0.59); without, it worsens at the end (0.91), and accuracy 2-3 moves from the goal falls from 67% to 58% as the flat share climbs to 28% - flat planning near the goal makes the student worse.
  • Neither matches people at any distance on these layouts: 70-74% optimal 2-3 moves from the goal (people 85-89%) and 30-34% at 7-9 (people 48% → 59%), and far less efficient (2.8-3.7 against 1.9-2.3) while matching people on the session's puzzles. The near-goal part is the student's own, not the layouts': the start network's intuition is 61% optimal 2-3 moves out on the session's puzzles too (58% on the human layouts).
  • So AND-OR earns its place: it lets the flat share start where people's does and still rise, and keeps the student learning and accurate near the goal. Caveats: one seed, 8 students per run; the without-AND-OR run's late decline may partly be its higher flat share, which is what it needed to start where people do.

Beyond the efficiency curve: does the two-mode student learn like people?¶

The session runs above against people on everything else that changes over a session: the curve in finer blocks, the gain per puzzle length, giving up and restarting, and how much individuals differ; and the snapshots on people's layouts by stage. People's figures are means over people (as the students' are over students); the session's puzzles are pool puzzles at people's lengths, people's are their own layouts.

In [29]:
STAGE_BOUNDS = [(1, 9), (10, 27), (28, 45), (46, 72)]
stage_of = lambda x: next(f"{a}-{b}" for a, b in STAGE_BOUNDS if a <= x <= b)


def session_records(run):
    """One row per puzzle of a session run (every student), with its stage of people's session."""
    d = json.load(open(os.path.join(paths.SESSIONS, run, "no_teacher", "sessions.json")))
    e = pd.DataFrame([dict(x, subject=s) for s, rec in d.items() for x in rec])
    return e.assign(stage=e.trial.map(stage_of), ratio=e.moves / e.distance)


people_t = hd.trials()
people_t = people_t[people_t.trial <= 72].assign(stage=lambda t: t.trial.map(stage_of),
                                                 ratio=lambda t: t.moves / t.distance,
                                                 restarted=lambda t: t.attempts > 1)
LEARNERS = {"people": people_t, "two-mode": session_records("lean_people_all_m10_ao"),
            "forward": session_records("lean_people_all_m10_noao")}
LEARNER_COLORS = {"people": INK, "two-mode": "#e6550d", "forward": "#e6a00d"}


def by_stage(d):
    """Per stage: means over individuals (people or students) of solving, giving up, restarting and moves / optimal
    on solved puzzles, the spread of moves / optimal across individuals, and moves / optimal per puzzle length."""
    rows = {}
    for st, g in d.groupby("stage", sort=False):
        w = g[g.solved]
        each = w.ratio.groupby(w.subject).mean()
        r = {"solved": g.groupby("subject").solved.mean().mean(),
             "gave up": g.groupby("subject").surrendered.mean().mean(),
             "restarted": g.groupby("subject").restarted.mean().mean() if "restarted" in g else 0.0,
             "moves / optimal": each.mean(), "sd across individuals": each.std()}
        for length, gl in w.groupby("distance"):
            r[f"length {length}"] = gl.ratio.groupby(gl.subject).mean().mean()
        rows[st] = r
    return pd.DataFrame(rows).T.loc[[f"{a}-{b}" for a, b in STAGE_BOUNDS]]


stages_table = pd.concat({k: by_stage(d) for k, d in LEARNERS.items()})
layouts = {}  # snapshots on people's 70 layouts, against the same stage of people

  • Where the two-mode student learns like people
    • How much and how fast. On solved puzzles in the session, moves / optimal falls 2.87 → 2.27 (people 2.77 → 2.17): the same 0.60. In blocks of 9 trials both fall fast over the first ~30 trials and then flatten (a).
    • On which puzzles, roughly. Both gain little on 6-move puzzles and most on 13-move ones (b: people 3.40 → 2.24, the student 3.72 → 2.81). In between they differ: on 10-move puzzles the student gains half as much as people (0.47 against 0.94), on 15-move ones a little more (0.78 against 0.60).
    • On people's layouts, in proportion. Its snapshots there cut moves / optimal by 20% (3.52 → 2.81); people on the same layouts cut it by 17% (2.32 → 1.93).
    • Revisits stay human. About 7% of its moves undo the last one throughout, against people's 5-6% (revisit misfit 0.05-0.07 at every stage).
  • Where it doesn't
    • Giving up and restarting run the other way (c). People restart 13-20% of puzzles and give up more late in the session (12% → 16%), so their solve rate falls at the end (88% → 84%). The student never restarts, gives up less as it improves (8% → 6%), and solves a flat 82-84%. Nothing in the model tires or loses patience.
    • Its level on people's layouts is too low. It gains in proportion but from far below them: 70-72% optimal 2-3 moves from the goal against people's 85-89%, and 3.5 → 2.8 moves / optimal against 2.3 → 1.9. Its session curve matches people's only on the pool puzzles its start was calibrated on, which are easier than people's layouts 7+ moves from the goal (the same network, on pool puzzles of people's lengths: 8-15 points more often optimal there). A start calibrated on people's own layouts (round 2 epoch 5 by intuition, which matches their first attempts and their skill by distance) fixes the level, but in the session it barely learns at any multiplier or training mix (experiments/session_fit.py → session_fit.csv).
    • Individuals hardly differ (d). Across people, whole-session moves / optimal spreads widely (a standard deviation of 0.6-1.4 per stage); across the 8 students, 0.07-0.17. Every student starts from the same network and differs only by chance: there are no fast or slow learners.
    • Part of the learning is imposed. The flat share rising from 8% to 18% is a schedule taken from the mixture fit, not something the student finds. The forward student, with the same kind of schedule and no AND-OR, gains less and stalls mid-session (2.88 → 2.36), but how much of the two-mode student's gain is the network's and how much the schedule's hasn't been separated.
    • Mid-puzzle skill (accepted as a limitation for now): 31-34% optimal 7-9 moves from the goal against people's 48% → 59%.
  • So the defensible claim is narrower than "learns like people": the two-mode student reproduces how much people improve, how fast and on which puzzles, but not their level on their own layouts, their giving up and restarting, or how much they differ from each other. Caveats: one seed, 8 students per run; people's later stages have fewer people (not everyone played 72 trials).

3. How this relates to the papers¶

  • van Opheusden et al. 2023 (four-in-a-row): best-first search over a feature-weighted value; expertise is mostly more search (depth 5 → 6) and fewer attention lapses (feature drop rate 0.23 → 0.17), with little change in heuristic quality. Consistent with relevance not mattering and search budget helping.
  • Collins et al. 2026 (new games): novices plan flat (every option one step deep, a goal-directed Boltzmann choice) and fast (a single simulated run). Section 2c's flat planner is this, with consideration limited to the policy's top few moves; its move-by-move mixture with intuition is their per-player mixture applied per stage.
  • Arbitration and metareasoning (Daw, Niv & Dayan 2005; Lee, Shimojo & O'Doherty 2014; Keramati et al. 2011; Kool, Gershman & Cushman 2017; Lieder & Griffiths 2017; Callaway et al. 2022): systems compete per decision by reliability or cost; computation is spent selectively. Means-ends analysis (Newell & Simon 1972) and plan-until-habit (Keramati et al. 2016) integrate backward subgoals or cached values into a single forward process; Anzai & Simon (1979) show strategies shifting with practice. Best of 8 (2b) has no counterpart in this literature.
  • Zhang et al. 2025 (failures of consideration): an imitation-trained network seeds forward Monte Carlo search and decides what gets considered; undervalued actions are never sampled. Matches "experience enters through proposals".

4. Open questions¶

  1. Relevance in proposals rather than evaluation: bias rollout moves toward relevant features.
  2. Novelty as pruning (Iterated Width): discard rollouts that reach nothing new and resample or search deeper, instead of falling back to a policy sample.
  3. Backward reasoning in people's moves: AND-OR is now in the mixture (strongest near the goal and on slow moves). Loops don't trigger it and no plan is carried out after a slow move: backward reasoning looks like one deliberated move at a time. Next: what triggers a slow move (the policy's uncertainty? the opening?); a boundary between modes on distance or on the blocking chain people can see; a hidden-state model of plan following, to rule it out properly.
  4. Mid-puzzle skill: the two-mode student learns people's efficiency curve, but no model reaches people's 48% → 59% optimal moves 7-9 from the goal. Candidates: training the value head on the student's own flat choices, a rule for when to use each mode (the policy's uncertainty, the blocking chain), or a flat share tied to the evaluator's reliability rather than a schedule.

Caveats: one start network, one round-3 network, one session run (seed 2); the session's held-out puzzles only; the sum score favours rollouts that move many cars.
